name: Combined vitamin K-dependent clotting factor deficiency (GGCX/VKORC1)
aliases: combined deficiency of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors

clinicalPearls: A rare autosomal recessive disorder causing concurrent deficiency of the vitamin K-dependent clotting factors II, VII, IX and X, and of proteins C and S
Bleeding varies from mild to severe and may present in the neonatal period with intracranial or umbilical bleeding, mimicking severe haemorrhagic disease of the newborn
Both the prothrombin time and the activated partial thromboplastin time are prolonged, reflecting the multiple factor deficiencies
GGCX variants can also cause skeletal and connective-tissue features, such as a pseudoxanthoma-elasticum-like phenotype, alongside the coagulopathy
Affected individuals show marked sensitivity to warfarin because the same vitamin K cycle enzymes are involved
Some patients respond, at least partially, to vitamin K because it drives residual carboxylase or reductase activity
Management uses vitamin K and, for acute or severe bleeding, replacement of the vitamin K-dependent factors
reference.pathophysiology: The vitamin K-dependent clotting factors require gamma-carboxylation of glutamate residues to become functional, a reaction catalysed by gamma-glutamyl carboxylase (GGCX) that consumes reduced vitamin K. Vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1) regenerates the reduced vitamin needed for this cycle. Loss-of-function variants in GGCX or VKORC1 impair carboxylation, so factors II, VII, IX and X, and the anticoagulant proteins C and S, are secreted as poorly functional undercarboxylated proteins. The dominant clinical effect is bleeding, and because the same enzymes are the target of coumarin anticoagulants, affected patients are hypersensitive to warfarin.
additionalDifferentials: Acquired vitamin K deficiency (malabsorption, poor intake, biliary obstruction)
Warfarin or other vitamin K antagonist effect, including inadvertent ingestion
Haemorrhagic disease of the newborn from vitamin K deficiency
Liver disease with impaired factor synthesis
Isolated inherited deficiency of a single vitamin K-dependent factor
additionalInvestigations: Prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time, both prolonged
Individual assays of factors II, VII, IX and X, and of proteins C and S
Response of clotting times to vitamin K administration
Measurement of undercarboxylated (des-gamma-carboxy) proteins where available
GGCX and VKORC1 gene analysis to confirm the diagnosis
Evaluation for skeletal or connective-tissue features in suspected GGCX defects
redFlags: Severe mucosal, gastrointestinal, or intra-abdominal bleeding
Marked bleeding provoked by a standard warfarin dose
Umbilical or postpartum bleeding suggesting a severe congenital coagulopathy
reference.prognosis: With vitamin K supplementation and factor replacement for acute bleeding, most patients achieve satisfactory haemostasis and a good long-term outlook. Severity depends on the residual enzyme activity, and neonatal presentations carry higher risk if not promptly recognised.
pitfalls: Attributing the coagulopathy solely to dietary vitamin K deficiency or occult warfarin exposure
Not recognising warfarin hypersensitivity, leading to over-anticoagulation
Overlooking associated skeletal or connective-tissue features in GGCX defects
Failing to check the response to vitamin K, which can guide management
references: Hoffman: Hematology - Basic Principles and Practice
management: High-dose vitamin K (phytomenadione), often lifelong, to drive residual carboxylase and reductase activity and restore factor function
Factor replacement with prothrombin complex concentrate or fresh frozen plasma for acute severe bleeding
Avoid coumarin anticoagulants, or use with extreme caution, given the marked warfarin hypersensitivity
Prompt recognition and treatment of neonatal bleeding, which can mimic severe haemorrhagic disease of the newborn
Monitor prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time and individual factor levels to guide dosing
Evaluate and manage skeletal and connective-tissue features in GGCX defects with relevant specialists
Genetic counselling and family screening given autosomal recessive inheritance
